title: Nondistinguished faces decrease the fillable squiggle rank
statement:
Let $\mathsf{Adj}$ be the nerve-enriched free strict adjunction, using the atomic string normal form of [lem-coef-adjunction-squiggle-normal-form] and the fillable arrows, depth $k$, child $a^-$ and parent $b^\dagger$ of [lem-coef-adjunction-fillable-parent-bijection]. For a fillable arrow $c$ define $\rho(c)=(w(c),k(c),\dim c)$, putting $k(\ell)=0$ for the unique fillable $0$-arrow. Order triples lexicographically, first by width, then depth, then dimension.

For every fillable $n$-arrow $a$ with $n\geq1$ and every $0\leq i\leq n$ other than its depth $k(a)$, decompose $d_i a$ into its unique word of degeneracies of nondegenerate atomic arrows. For each nondegenerate atomic factor $b$ in that word, put $g(b)=b$ if $b$ is fillable, and $g(b)=b^\dagger$ otherwise. Then $\rho(g(b))<\rho(a)$. An identity face has an empty word, so the assertion includes that case.

source.place: Proof of Proposition 4.2.15, nondistinguished-face analysis, pp. 839--840; its two main cases i not equal to k-1,k and i=k-1, with both reduction subcases Read online; archival copy WANTED. No Stacks tag states this combinatorial result.

proof.text: Write $w=w(a)$ and $k=k(a)$. By [lem-coef-adjunction-squiggle-normal-form], compute $d_i a$ by applying $q_i(t)=t$ for $t\leq i$ and $q_i(t)=t-1$ for $t>i$, where the old alphabet is $0,\ldots,n+1$, and then cancelling equal adjacent pairs. Each cancellation deletes two letters, hence decreases width by two. Cut the reduced string at its endpoint symbols to obtain its atomic factors; widths add under concatenation. To remove degeneracies from a factor, list its distinct internal numerical letters $t_1<\cdots<t_r$ and replace $t_j$ by $j$. This leaves width unchanged, makes its dimension $r\leq n-1$, and replaces any retained numerical letter $t_j$ by $j\leq t_j$. These operations give exactly the nondegenerate factors specified in the statement, by uniqueness of the normal form. By [lem-coef-adjunction-fillable-parent-bijection], for every such factor $b$, $w(g(b))\leq w(b)+1$: a fillable factor is unchanged, a nonfillable factor with target $-$ has a parent of the same width, and one with target $+$ has a parent of width one greater.

source.place: Coordinate preliminaries for the factor decomposition in Proposition 4.2.15, pp. 839--840; normal form and parent formulas from the two cited nodes

proof.text: First suppose $i\ne k-1,k$. The two levels identified by $q_i$ are disjoint from $k$. Consequently the first internal letter becomes $k'=k-1$ if $i<k-1$, and $k'=k$ if $i>k$; in either case $1\leq k'\leq n-1$. Since $k$ occurred only once, $k'$ still occurs only once. No cancellation can delete this letter, because deleting a letter requires an equal neighbour. The initial $-$ cannot cancel either: the surviving $k'$ separates it from the rest of the string. Thus the first atomic factor contains this internal letter and has width at least two. On removing its degeneracies, its nondegenerate factor $b_1$ still has target $-$ and a unique first internal letter, hence is fillable by [lem-coef-adjunction-fillable-parent-bijection]. Step 1 gives $w(b_1)\leq w$, $k(b_1)\leq k'\leq k$, and $\dim b_1\leq n-1$. If width drops, the first rank coordinate drops; otherwise depth drops or stays equal, and in the latter case dimension drops. Therefore $\rho(g(b_1))=\rho(b_1)<\rho(a)$.

source.place: Proposition 4.2.15, p. 839, first bullet: the first atomic factor when the face index is neither depth nor depth minus one

proof.text: Still in the case of step 2, every further atomic factor $b_j$ has $w(b_j)\leq w-2$: the first factor already contributes at least two to the total reduced width, which is at most $w$, and all other widths are nonnegative. Step 1 and the parent-width formula of [lem-coef-adjunction-fillable-parent-bijection] give $w(g(b_j))\leq w(b_j)+1\leq w-1<w$. This proves the required strict lexicographic inequality for all remaining factors, regardless of their targets, degeneracies, or fillability.

source.place: Proposition 4.2.15, p. 839, first bullet: later factors have width at most the original width minus two

proof.text: It remains to take $i=k-1$. If $w=2$, atomicity and nondegeneracy force $a=(-,1,-)$ and $n=k=1$: there is only one internal letter, and every numerical level must occur. Applying $q_0$ gives $(-,-,-)$, which reduces to the singleton identity $(-)$. Its atomic word is empty, so there is nothing to check. Positive dimension excludes $w=1$. Hence in all remaining cases $w>2$, and $a_2$ is internal; strict alternation gives $1\leq a_2<k$, so $k\geq2$.

source.place: Proposition 4.2.15, p. 839, second bullet: the width-two counit and the bound on depth for larger width

proof.text: Suppose $i=k-1$ and $a_2=k-1$. The map $q_{k-1}$ identifies the adjacent letters $a_1=k$ and $a_2=k-1$, so at least one equal pair is cancelled. Thus the reduced width is at most $w-2$. Since $k\geq2$ and $k\leq n$, this face map identifies two internal levels, and no internal letter becomes an endpoint symbol. Reductions introduce no new letters. The result is therefore either an identity, whose word is empty, or a single atomic arrow. In the latter case remove its degeneracies to obtain $b$ of width at most $w-2$. The width bound from step 1, using [lem-coef-adjunction-fillable-parent-bijection], gives $w(g(b))\leq w-1<w$, as required. This also covers further cancellations and loss of numerical levels during reduction.

source.place: Proposition 4.2.15, pp. 839--840, second bullet, subcase where the first internal letter is one above the second

proof.text: Finally suppose $i=k-1$ and $a_2<k-1$. The only distinct letters merged by $q_{k-1}$ are $k-1,k$. The unique occurrence of $k$ is at position 1, whose neighbours are $-$ and $a_2<k-1$. Hence the mapped string has no equal adjacent pair and needs no reduction. Its width is $w$. Both merged levels are internal, so it remains atomic with target $-$. Every new numerical level occurs, since every old numerical level occurred and $q_{k-1}$ maps the old internal levels onto the new ones. Thus this face $b=d_{k-1}a$ is nondegenerate of dimension $n-1$. Nondegeneracy of $a$ also supplies an occurrence of $k-1$; it is neither $a_1$ nor $a_2$, hence is at a position greater than 2. After applying $q_{k-1}$, the first internal letter $k-1$ therefore occurs again, so $b$ is nonfillable. Its target is $-$, so [lem-coef-adjunction-fillable-parent-bijection] gives $w(b^\dagger)=w$ and $k(b^\dagger)=b_1=k-1$. Consequently $\rho(g(b))=\rho(b^\dagger)<\rho(a)$ by the second coordinate. This is the only atomic factor. Together with steps 2--5, these cases exhaust $i\ne k$ and every factor in its normal word.

source.place: Proposition 4.2.15, p. 840, final subcase: no reduction, repeated initial level, and parent of depth one smaller

The statement is the source's 'a.delta^l in A_{i-1} for l != k' written factorwise through the lexicographic (w,k,n) rank, which is exactly what the parent uses; it is not weakened and it restates no parent clause. Step 1: face, deletion, concatenation and compression facts all come from the normal-form statement, and w(g(b)) <= w(b)+1 comes from the parent formula. Steps 2-3 (i not k-1 or k): the unique letter k' = q_i(k) satisfies 1 <= k' <= n-1, which I checked at i=0 and i=n. It cannot be deleted, so the first factor is fillable with rank (<=w, <=k, <=n-1), and later factors have width <= w-2, so their parents have width <= w-1. Step 4 (elementary): width 2 forces a = epsilon, whose face d_0 is an identity; otherwise k >= 2. Step 5 (a_2 = k-1): a pair cancels, so the result is at most one atomic factor of width <= w-2. Step 6 (a_2 < k-1): no reduction, width w, nondegenerate and nonfillable, and its parent has depth k-1. Steps 5-6 are the source's two subcases. Independent enumeration over n <= 5, w <= 9: all 9898 factor inequalities hold (one empty-word face), and (a^-)^dagger = a holds for all 1255 fillable arrows. There are no new nodes.
